title: The Better Word for This Painting Didn't Exist Until 1910
standfirst: In 1894, the year Claude Monet was still reworking his thirty-odd canvases of Rouen Cathedral's west front, Maurice Prendergast came through the same city and pointed his brush at an ordinary street instead. Both paintings are catalogued today under the same word, Impressionism — a word historians apply to only one of them without an argument.

sections.heading: A Street Corner in the Year Monet Wouldn't Leave the Cathedral Alone
sections.body: Claude Monet spent the early months of 1892 and 1893 in a rented room across the square from Rouen Cathedral, painting its west front over and over from the same window at different hours and in different weather. He kept reworking the results in his studio through 1894 — more than thirty canvases in total — before choosing twenty for a show at his dealer Paul Durand-Ruel's Paris gallery in May 1895. He sold eight of them before the exhibition closed; Camille Pissarro and Paul Cézanne both came to look and praised what they saw. Sometime in that same middle year, 1894, Maurice Prendergast came through Rouen too, with a sketchbook and a box of watercolors, and set up somewhere that wasn't the cathedral square. What he made is a sheet barely the size of a hardback book, about 33 by 22 centimetres, now in a private collection — catalogued, like Monet's cathedrals, under a single shared word: Impressionism. Whether that word fits both painters equally is a separate question, and for Prendergast, most historians now say no.

sections.heading: He Learned to Paint by Sketching Cafés, Not Copying Casts
sections.body: Maurice Brazil Prendergast was born in St. John's, Newfoundland, on 10 October 1858; when his father's grocery business failed three years later, the family resettled in Boston, and Maurice spent years doing commercial design work before he could afford formal art training. He sailed for Paris in January 1891, already in his thirties, and enrolled at two academies at once: the Académie Julian, where Jean-Paul Laurens taught, and the Académie Colarossi, under Gustave Courtois and Jean-Joseph Benjamin-Constant. Both schools built their teaching around copying plaster casts; Prendergast mostly ignored that part of the arrangement. He drew live models in the studio in the mornings, then spent his afternoons in cafés and along the boulevards, sketching whoever walked past. That habit — watching strangers in public, fast, in a notebook — became the entire engine of his career: the thing that eventually produced beach scenes, park scenes, and, in 1894, a street in Rouen with nobody in it he would ever paint again.

sections.heading: The Sketches That Got Him Into Print Weren't Signed With His Name
sections.body: In 1893, while Prendergast was still living and working in Paris, several of his watercolor sketches were stolen from his studio. They surfaced anyway, selected for reproduction that same year in the London magazine The Studio — but under the name Michael Dignam, not his own. Readers who saw them in print had no way of knowing whose hand had actually made them. The record doesn't say who Dignam was, whether he ever admitted where the sketches came from, or whether Prendergast got any public acknowledgment once the theft came to light; what survives is the bare fact of it. The timing is what makes it sting: this happened during the same few years he was building the sketching habit — live models in the morning, boulevards in the afternoon — that would carry him through the rest of his career, Rouen included. A young, still-unknown American having his best early work published under a stranger's name is exactly the kind of detail that gets smoothed out of the tidy version of an artist's life, and here it hasn't been.

sections.heading: The Word on This Painting's Label Didn't Exist Yet
sections.body: Prendergast's closest friend in these Paris years was the Canadian painter James Wilson Morrice, who introduced him to the English avant-garde, Walter Sickert and Aubrey Beardsley among them. Wikipedia's account credits a further acquaintance with Édouard Vuillard and Pierre Bonnard, made during this same 1891–95 stay, with pushing him firmly toward Post-Impressionism; Britannica tells a different story, dating the Vuillard connection and his pointillist leanings to a second Paris trip around 1899, five years after the Rouen watercolor. The two accounts don't agree on when it happened, only that it did. Either way, Britannica now classifies Prendergast outright as a Post-Impressionist — one of the first American painters to work in the broad, flattened colour the label describes — not an Impressionist at all. The trouble is that neither label was a clean choice in 1894. Post-Impressionism wasn't coined until the critic Roger Fry needed a word for his 1910 London exhibition, Manet and the Post-Impressionists, sixteen years after Prendergast set up in Rouen. Whoever filed this watercolor under Impressionism wasn't wrong so much as working with the only word on the shelf at the time.

sections.heading: The Man Who Watched Crowds for a Living Began Losing the Ability to Hear Them
sections.body: Prendergast never married; he lived with his younger brother Charles, also a painter, for the rest of his life. Charles ran a frame-making business that did more than pay bills — it put wealthy collectors in direct contact with Maurice's watercolors and oils, and the two brothers' finances stayed tied together for decades. By 1905 Maurice had developed severe hearing problems. He joined the L Street Brownies, a Boston open-water swimming club, on the theory that cold-water swimming and sun exposure might slow the decline; neither that nor anything medicine offered worked, and his hearing eventually went entirely. He kept painting anyway, through what turned out to be the last decade of his life — he died in 1924 — producing the increasingly abstract, mosaic-like oils he is now best known for. It is a strange arc for a man whose early reputation rested on watching strangers closely enough to catch how they stood, dressed, and moved through a public street: the observing kept working long after the listening had stopped.

sections.heading: His Own Exhibition Group Wasn't Sure Where to Put Him Either
sections.body: In 1908 Prendergast showed with The Eight at New York's Macbeth Galleries, a group organised in protest at the National Academy of Design's exhibition juries. Robert Henri and the other Ashcan realists in that lineup painted saloons, tenements, and boxing matches in dark, gritty colour; Prendergast's jewel-toned, pattern-flattened crowd scenes sat awkwardly beside them, and a Newark Evening News critic that year wrote that he did "not think that Prendergast has spoken the final word with his Cézanne technique" — a backhanded way of admitting nobody was sure what to call him yet. Five years later he showed seven works at the 1913 Armory Show, the exhibition that introduced European modernism to American audiences wholesale, and his reception improved after that. He is now credited as one of the first Americans to champion Cézanne's work at all, and as a figure who helped import Post-Impressionism into American painting years before most of his countrymen had a name for it. Which leaves the plain word "Impressionism" sitting on a small Rouen street scene looking less like an argument than a label nobody has gone back to fix.
